content: All equipment, supplies, and receptacles that come into contact with the BCG vaccine must be treated and disposed of as biohazardous materials. The pharmacist or individual responsible for preparing the vaccine should wear gloves and take precautions to avoid contact with the BCG vaccine, especially if they have broken skin. If preparation cannot be performed in a biocontainment hood, a mask and gown should be worn to prevent inhalation of BCG organisms and accidental exposure to broken skin. Using aseptic techniques, 1 mL of sterile water for injection (USP) at a temperature of 4–25°C (39–77°F) should be added to a vial of the vaccine. The vial should be gently swirled until a homogeneous suspension is achieved. Vigorous shaking should be avoided, as it may cause clumping of the mycobacteria. Individuals administering the vaccine must take necessary precautions to minimize the risk of disease transmission. Hands should be washed before attending to each new patient. Syringes and needles used for vaccine administration must be sterile and preferably disposable to reduce the risk of contamination. A separate needle and syringe should be used for each application. Disposable needles and the multiple puncture device must be discarded as biohazardous waste in labeled, puncture-proof containers to prevent accidental needlestick injuries or reuse. After use, any unused vaccine and all materials exposed to the product should be immediately placed in a biohazard container and disposed of appropriately. The reconstituted vaccine should be stored in a refrigerator, protected from direct sunlight, and used within 2 hours. Freezing the reconstituted product is not recommended. The contents of the BCG vaccine vial should not be filtered. Care should be taken to avoid exposing the vaccine to direct sunlight, and bacteriostatic solutions must not be used. Parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration whenever the solution and container allow. Reconstitution should result in a uniform suspension of the bacilli. BCG vaccination is reserved for individuals who exhibit a reaction of less than 5 mm induration after skin testing with 5 TU of PPD tuberculin. It is recommended that a Mantoux skin test be performed prior to BCG vaccination to confirm the absence of tuberculosis infection. The vaccine should only be administered after fully explaining the risks and benefits to the vaccinee, parent, or guardian. BCG vaccination should not be given to individuals previously infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The vaccine is administered percutaneously using a sterile multiple puncture device. This device consists of a plastic holder containing a thin, wafer-like stainless steel plate (7/8 by 1 1/8) with 36 protruding points. After the vaccine is prepared, the skin site is cleansed with an alcohol or acetone sponge and allowed to dry thoroughly. There is limited information available regarding the monitoring of BCG vaccine administration in the drug label. Similarly, there is limited information on the intravenous compatibility of the BCG vaccine. Accidental overdoses, if treated promptly with anti-tuberculous drugs, have not resulted in complications. If the vaccination response is allowed to progress, it can still be successfully treated with anti-tuberculous drugs, but complications may include regional adenitis, lupus vulgaris, subcutaneous cold abscesses, ocular lesions, and others. The BCG vaccine for percutaneous use is a live, attenuated culture preparation of the Bacillus of Calmette and Guérin (BCG) strain of Mycobacterium bovis. The TICE® strain used in this vaccine was developed at the University of Illinois from a strain originally obtained from the Pasteur Institute. The medium used to grow the TICE® BCG organism for the preparation of the freeze-dried cake contains glycerin, asparagine, citric acid, potassium phosphate, magnesium sulfate, and iron ammonium citrate. The final preparation prior to freeze-drying also contains lactose. The freeze-dried BCG preparation is delivered in vials, each containing 1 to 8 × 10⁸ colony-forming units (CFU) of BCG, equivalent to approximately 50 mg wet weight. In-vitro potency is determined through colony counts derived from a serial dilution assay, and intradermal guinea pig testing is also used as an indirect measure of potency. Reconstitution of the vaccine requires the addition of sterile water for injection (USP) at 4–25°C (39–77°F). For an adult dosage, 1 mL of sterile water for injection should be added to one vial of vaccine. For a pediatric dosage, 2 mL of sterile water for injection should be added to one vial of vaccine. No preservatives have been added to the vaccine. Tuberculosis (TB) is primarily an airborne communicable disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. TB remains a significant global public health issue, with an estimated 8–10 million cases and 2–3 million deaths occurring annually. In the United States, TB control has been a persistent challenge, particularly with the resurgence of TB in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Since nationwide reporting began in 1953, TB incidence in the U.S. had declined by approximately 6% per year until the resurgence. By the early 1990s, TB incidence rates began to decline again, with a 26% decrease since the peak in 1992. During the 1990s, drug-resistant TB emerged as a significant public health concern. Approximately 2% of TB patients were infected with strains resistant to both isoniazid and rifampin (multi-drug-resistant TB, or MDR-TB). Most individuals infected with M. tuberculosis remain infected for many years, developing latent infections. Active TB reactivates in 5–15% of immunocompetent individuals during their lifetime. Without treatment, active TB is fatal in approximately 50% of cases.
